nodes.name: Truthful but non-monotone SWAC\xspace
nodes.statement: Consider a SWACxspace\ where the agent's valuation is uniform over the range [0,8]. The auction proceeds as follows: item For bids below 4, the agent rents the asset for six days, and pays 2 each day, for a total of 12. item For bids 4 and above, the agent rents the asset for five days, and pays 4 upfront on the first day and zero on the remaining days. Under the first offer, the overall utility at the end of the rental period for an agent with valuation v is 6v - 12, and under the second offer it is 5v - 4. Thus, all agents in our distribution would derive higher overall utility from the second offer compared to the first. However, stagewise-IRxspace\ agents with v<4 would not accept the second offer, because their utility on the first day would be negative (v - 4 < 0). Only agents with valuation at least 4 can accept the second offer; the high payment on the first day filters out agents with lower valuations. It is not hard to see that this mechanism is truthfulfootnote Agents with valuations below 4 cannot bid geq 4, and all other bids yield the same result as bidding truthfully. Agents with valuations geq 4 prefer the second offer, and this can be achieved by bidding truthfully. . However, it is non-monotone in the agent valuation with respect to both the allocation (i.e., the number of rental days) and the revenue of the designer: agents with valuation 3 receive an allocation of six days and net the designer a revenue of 12, while agents with valuation 4 receive an allocation of five days and net the designer a revenue of 4.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{ex:intro-example}
    Consider a SWAC\xspace\ 
    where the agent's valuation is uniform over the range $[0,8]$.
    The auction proceeds as follows:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item For bids below $4$, the agent rents the asset for six days, and pays $2$
        each day, for a total of $12$.
         \item For bids $4$ and above, the agent rents the asset for five days, and pays $4$ upfront on the first day and zero on the remaining days.
    \end{enumerate}
    Under the first offer, the overall utility at the end of the rental period for an agent with valuation $v$ is $6v - 12$,
    and under the second offer it is $5v - 4$.
    Thus, all agents in our distribution would derive higher overall utility from the second offer  compared to the first. However, stagewise-IR\xspace\ agents with $v<4$ would not accept the second offer,
    because their utility on the first day would be negative
    ($v - 4 < 0$).
    Only agents with valuation at least $4$ can accept the second offer; the high payment on the first day \emph{filters out} agents with lower valuations.
    
    It is not hard to see that this mechanism is
    \emph{truthful}\footnote{
    Agents with valuations below $4$ cannot bid $\geq 4$, and all other bids yield the same result as bidding truthfully. Agents with valuations $\geq 4$ prefer the second offer, and this can be achieved by bidding truthfully.
    }.
    However, it is
    \emph{non-monotone in the agent valuation}
    with respect to both the allocation (i.e., the number of rental days)
    and the revenue of the designer:
    agents with valuation $3$ receive an allocation of six days and net the designer a revenue of $12$,
    while agents with valuation $4$ receive an allocation of five days and net the designer a revenue of $4$.

nodes.statement: The first step in our reduction is to show that w.l.o.g., an optimal rental mechanism is a fixed (i.e., predetermined) sequence of SWACsxspace: because agent valuations are independent of one another, an optimal rental mechanism can be history-independent, meaning that although we do not know in advance whether the asset will be available to rent on a given day and what we did with the asset prior to that day, we can decide in advance what the mechanism should do if the asset is available that day, regardless of the history up to that day.
nodes.raw_latex:
The first step in our reduction is to show that w.l.o.g.,
an optimal rental mechanism is a \emph{fixed} (i.e., predetermined) sequence of SWACs\xspace:
because agent valuations are independent of one another,
an optimal rental mechanism can be \emph{history-independent},
meaning that 
although we do not know in advance whether the asset will be available to rent on a given day and what we did with the asset prior to that day,

nodes.statement: Let g be a reward function matching the conditions of the lemma. Since g is payment-independent, in this proof we abuse notation and write g(v) instead of g(v,cdot). Consider an agent vinV. Since the designer's reward depends only on the number of units sold to the agent, an allocation that would maximize the designer's reward is in X_v=argmaxxinsqrrangensetxcdot g(v)-c(x). Note that we don't yet know this allocation is implementable, meaning that we don't know we can achieve this allocation by a truthful auction. For any valuations w<v and allocations x_winX_w and x_vinX_v, it holds that: &treww=x_wcdot g(w)-c(x_w)geq x_vcdot g(w)-c(x_v)\\ &trewv= x_vcdot g(v)-c(x_v)geq x_wcdot g(v)-c(x_w) Rearranging the above equations, we get that (x_w-x_v)g(w)geq c(x_w)-c(x_v) geq (x_w-x_v)g(v). Suppose x_w>x_v. Since g is non-decreasing in the valuation, Eq.~() yields g(w)=g(v). Define an allocation rule alloc'(v)=minX_v, where we choose the largest allocation that maximizes the designer's reward for agent v. If alloc'(w)>alloc'(v) we would have g(w)=g(v), therefore X_w=X_v and in particular alloc'(w)=alloc'(v), which is a contradiction. Thus alloc' is a monotone (weakly) increasing allocation rule, and due to Myerson it can be implemented as a truthful fixed-ratexspace SWACxspace; given an agent, we ask them to reveal their bid, then sell alloc'(v) units at the total price of the unique payment rule, such that the payments are fixed-ratexspace over all days. Since it is a fixed-ratexspace SWACxspace, stagewise-IRxspace has no affect here and thus Myerson guarantees that this is truthful, and this proves point~ from the theorem. Let aucA be an optimal and truthful (n,D,g,c)-stagewise auction. Define S=settvinVxvnotinX_v. For all vinS we know that trew[aucA]v is less than the designer's reward from v in an optimal auction, and for all vnotinS we know trew[aucA]v is as high as possible. Thus since aucA is optimal we know Pr[S]=0. item We will prove that aucA is weakly-allocation-monotonexspace, for point~ of the proof. Let w,vinVsetminusS such that w<v and trew[aucA]wneq trew[aucA]v. We need to prove xwleqxv. Suppose xw>xv. In this case, as we proved above, g(w)=g(v). Suppose w,vinVsetminusS but trew[aucA]w=trew[aucA]v (the case of inequality is complete, due to point~). In this case equation~() yields trew[aucA]w=xwg(w)-c(xw)=trew[aucA]vgeqxwg(v)-c(xw), giving either xw=0, which is enough for allocation-monotonexspace, or g(w)=g(v). If g is strictly increasing, we are done, so suppose c is strictly increasing. In this case one of the inequalities from eq.~() is strict, proving that xw<xv, and completing the proof of point~. item Consider w,vinVsetminusS. From equation~() and due to the monotonicity of g, we have trew[aucA]v&=xvcdot g(v)-c(xv) geq xwcdot g(v)-c(xw) \\&geq xwcdot g(w)-c(xw)=trew[aucA]w and we are done.

If there is some winC for which trew[aucA]w=B, we can define v_i=w for all i, v^*=w and x^*=xw; this sequence fulfills all the required properties. Suppose B is not reached by any winC. Since B is a supremum (and not a maximum), there is a sequence of distinct elements sety_i_i=1^inftysubseteqC such that settrew[aucA]y_i_i=1^infty is strictly increasing, and limlimits_irightarrowinfty trew[aucA]y_i=B. We will find a subsequence of bracketsy_i that will match the require properties. For each allocation kinsqrrangen, define sety_i^k_i=1^inftysubseteqsety_i_i=1^infty to be the subsequence of the elements that are allocated k units in aucA (while preserving the original order from bracketsy_i). nodes.statement: Let aucA be a truthful SWACxspace w.r.t. revenue-like reward g(v,p)=alpha p, let CsubseteqV, and define B=sup trew[aucA]C. Let bracketsv_i be the sequence from Claim~ with its limit v^* and allocation x[aucA]v_i=x^*. Define a set S^astcoloneqsettvinVv>v^*textnormal and trew[aucA]v<B. The main effect we want from aucA' is to strictly increase the designer's reward from agents in S^ast, while making sure no other agent yields worse reward. To cause agents in S^* to change their bid and give us improved reward, we remove S^* from the bidding space --- but that is not enough, as agents in S^* may change their bid to a valuation that yields lower reward. To prevent this, we must also block off two types of bids: item Bids w > v^* that yield lower reward than B: textscRemRt=settwinVw>v^*textnormal but trew[aucA]w< B. This includes the set S^*. item Bids w < v^* that receive a higher allocation than x^*: textscRemLft=settwinVw<v^*textnormal but x[aucA]w > x^*. These bids must be removed to prevent agents in textscRemRt (including S^*) from bidding values lower than v^*, as we show below. Formally, we define aucA' as follows: The bid space of aucA' will be bracketsVcupsetv^*setminusbracketstextscRemLftcuptextscRemRt, and: item For bid v^*, the designer of aucA' will sell x^* units at a total price of limlimits_irightarrowinftyp[aucA]v_i, with fixed-ratexspace payments. item For all other bids, aucA' will offer exactly the same allocation and payment schedule as aucA for the same bid. Note that indeed limlimits_irightarrowinfty p[aucA]v_i is defined, since the sequence setp[aucA]v_i_i=1^infty is increasing and bounded from above: every element p[aucA]v_i is bounded by x^* v_i due to IR, therefore the whole sequence is bounded by x^* v_1. In Figure~ we can see an example of such a transformation from aucA to aucA', assuming v_i=v^* for all i, for ease of exposition. [H] [t]0.49textwidth includegraphics[width=textwidth]figures/fig3_1.PNG captionPart 1: Removing points in textscRemRt from the bidding set, that is, the points >v^* with a reward less than B=trew[aucA]v^* [t]0.49textwidth includegraphics[width=textwidth]figures/fig3_2.PNG captionPart 2: Removing points in textscRemLft from the bidding set, that is, the points <v^* with an allocation larger than x^* caption[An illustration of the transformation used for proofs for revenue-like reward]An illustration of the transformation from aucA to aucA'. We show for the points in V, the reward the designer yields from them in aucA in Subfigure~, and their allocation in aucA, in Subfigure~. On these figures we point out which valuations will be omitted from the bidding set of aucA'. What is the designer's reward in aucA'? Besides for v^*, agents who don't change their bid between aucA and aucA' still yield the same designer reward, because their outcome is the same. Thus we restrict the analysis to agents who change their bid. There are only a few reasons an agent may change their bid: if their bid in aucA was removed; if their bid was changed, in the case of agent v^*; or if they have a new and better option in aucA' --- this could only be bidding v^* as no other bid was added or changed. Before analyzing these cases, observe that rew[aucA']cdotv^*&=alphap[aucA']v^*-cbracketsx[aucA']v^*=alphabracketslimlimits_irightarrowinftyp[aucA]v_i-c(x^*)\\ &=limlimits_irightarrowinftybracketsalphap[aucA]v_i-c(x[aucA]v_i)=limlimits_irightarrowinfty trew[aucA]v_i=B.addtocounterequation1tagtheequation We now analyze each individual case, to show how the reward from each agent changes between aucA and aucA'. item Agent v^* will be truthful in aucA' (assuming v^*inV), as we show in each case: item If x[aucA']v^*=x[aucA]v^* and p[aucA']v^*=p[aucA]v^*: Since util[aucA']v^*v^*=util[aucA]v^*v^*, and there's no other bid with an increase in the designer's revenue from aucA to aucA', the tie-breaking does not change and agent v^* bids v^* in aucA'. item Else, let u be the new bid of v^* in aucA', and suppose uneq v^*. By the definition of aucA', util[aucA']v^*v^*&=xhat[aucA']v^*v^*-p[aucA']v^*=limlimits_irightarrowinftybracketsx[aucA]v_iv_i-p[aucA]v_i=limlimits_irightarrowinftyutil[aucA]v_iv_i\\ &geqlimlimits_irightarrowinftyutil[aucA]v_iv^*=limlimits_irightarrowinftybracketsx[aucA]v^*v_i-p[aucA]v^*=x[aucA]v^*v^*-p[aucA]v^*\\ &=util[aucA]v^*v^*gequtil[aucA]v^*u=util[aucA']v^*u, where the inequalities are due to the truthfulness of aucA. In particular we get that util[aucA']v^*v^*geq util[aucA]v^*v^*, which means that v^* can get nonnegative utility in aucA'. Additionally this equation shows that util[aucA']v^*v^*geq util[aucA']v^*u; thus the only reason for v^* to deviate from v^* to u is if rew[aucA']cdotu>rew[aucA']cdotv^*=B. But rew[aucA']cdotu=trew[aucA]u and rew[aucA']cdotv^*geq trew[aucA]v^*, so in this case agent v^* would also bid u in aucA, which is a contradiction to the truthfulness of aucA. Therefore, v^* also bids truthfully in aucA'. Thus trew[aucA']v^*=Bgeqtrew[aucA]w, by Eq.~ and definition of B. item If w<v^*: item If wintextscRemLft, since x[aucA]w>x^* then by Prop.~, we have util[aucA]ww<utilformula[aucA]wv_i for all i. Taking the limit, and since there is no filter on bid v^* in aucA', it holds that util[aucA]ww<util[aucA']wv^*, thus w will bid v^* in aucA'; there is no other new option for w. Hence trew[aucA']w=rew[aucA']cdotv^*=B. item Else, wnotintextscRemLft so it is possible for w to bid truthfully in aucA', in which case trew[aucA']w=trew[aucA]w. If agent w does not bid truthfully, it would only be to change their bid to v^*, in which case trew[aucA']w=B. item If w>v^*, item If wnotintextscRemRt, they only possible non-truthful bid is to bid v^*. This will not happen, since p[aucA']v^*geqp[aucA]v_i for all i, and in particular for some v_j<w. Thus, by the truthfulness of w in aucA, we know util[aucA']ww=util[aucA]wwgequtil[aucA]wv_jgequtil[aucA']wv^*. All in all, if wnotintextscRemRt, indeed trew[aucA']w=trew[aucA]w. item If wintextscRemRt, then trew[aucA]w<B. Since v^* would be truthful in aucA', then by Prop.~ and by removal of textscRemLft we know that if agent w bids below v^* this can only be to some bid with allocation x^*. But due to Prop.~ there is no reason for agent w to prefer the lower bid over v^*. Since we showed now that w bids geqv^*, by design of aucA' we have trew[aucA']wgeq B>trew[aucA]w. Also note that since w>v^*, agent w can get nonnegative utility in aucA', since util[aucA']wv^*gequtil[aucA']v^*v^*geq 0. In all the different cases, we showed that the agent has a bid in aucA' that yields nonnegative utility, which proves that aucA' is indeed IR.

nodes.statement: Let aucA be a truthful and optimal SWACxspace with respect to revenue-like reward. We will find a set that when removed, imposes monotonicity of the reward on the remaining valuations. We then show that if this set is of positive measure, we could create a SWACxspace with higher expected reward, which would contradict the optimality of aucA. For all xinsqrrangen define &S_x=settvinVx[aucA]v=xtextnormal, exists winVtextnormal s.t. w<vtextnormal and trew[aucA]w>trew[aucA]v,textnormal and\\ &S=bigcup_x=0^n S_x=settvinVexists winVtextnormal s.t. w<vtextnormal and trew[aucA]w>trew[aucA]v. Observe that for all w,vinVsetminusS such that w<v, necessarily trew[aucA]wleq trew[aucA]v, because otherwise v would be in S. Suppose that aucA is not reward-monotonexspace, so Pr[S]>0. Since S is a finite union of sets, thus there is some S_x with PrsqbrS_x>0. Define a set UsubseteqS_x in the following manner: item If there is some vinS_x with Pr[v]>0 (in the case of a distribution with a point mass), define Ucoloneq setv and get Pr[U]>0. By definition of S_x, there is some valuation w<v=minU such that trew[aucA]w>trew[aucA]v. item Else, we can choose some uinS_x such that UcoloneqsettvinS_xvgeq u has Pr[U]>0. Since uinS_x there is a valuation w<u with trew[aucA]w>trew[aucA]u. Thus, due to Prop.~ and since the reward is valuation-independent, we have that also trew[aucA]w>trew[aucA]v for all vinU. Define Ccoloneq settwinVw<minU, and note that the minimum does indeed exist either way U was defined. Let aucA' be the SWACxspace from Claim~ over C. See Figure~ for an illustration. [h] includegraphics[width=0.8linewidth]figures/violation.png caption[Illustration of the reward-monotonicity violation found in the proof of reward monotonicity for revenue-like reward]The reward-monotonicity violation, in the form of the set U and the sequence v_0, v_1, ldots rightarrow v^* whose rewards approach B. We will show that: item aucA' is individually rational, item for all winV, trew[aucA']wgeq trew[aucA]w, and item for all winU it holds that trew[aucA']w>trew[aucA]w. Let $\auc{A}$ be an optimal truthful SWAC\xspace with respect to revenue-like reward. Due to  Lemma~\ref{lemma:rev-like-rmono}, $\auc{A}$ is reward-monotone\xspace. Let $\mathcal{V}_1$ be the remaining set from the definition, such that $\Pr\sqbr{\mathcal{V}_1}=1$ and for all valuations $w,v\in\mathcal{V}_1$, if $w<v$ then $\trew[\auc{A}]{w}\leq \trew[\auc{A}]{v}$. 
    
    Define the following sets for all $x\in\sqrrange{n}$:    
    \begin{align*}
        &\mathcal{T}_x=\sett{w\in\mathcal{V}_1}{\x[\auc{A}]{w}=x\textnormal{, }\exists v\in\mathcal{V}_1\textnormal{ s.t. } w<v\textnormal{, }x>\x[\auc{A}]{v}\textnormal{ and }\trew[\auc{A}]{w}<\trew[\auc{A}]{v}},\\
        &\mathcal{T}=\bigcup_{x=0}^n \mathcal{T}_x=\sett{w\in\mathcal{V}_1}{\exists v\in\mathcal{V}_1\textnormal{ s.t. }w<v\textnormal{, }\x[\auc{A}]{w}>\x[\auc{A}]{v}\textnormal{ and }\trew[\auc{A}]{w}<\trew[\auc{A}]{v}}.
    \end{align*}

    Observe that for all $w,v\in\mathcal{V}_1\setminus\mathcal{T}$, it holds that $\trew[\auc{A}]{w}\leq \trew[\auc{A}]{v}$, and if this inequality is strict, then $\x[\auc{A}]{w}\leq\x[\auc{A}]{v}$ (because otherwise $w$ would be in $\mathcal{T}$). Therefore, if $\Pr[\mathcal{T}]=0$ we have that $\auc{A}$ is weakly-allocation-monotone\xspace and we are done.
    Suppose otherwise; since $\mathcal{T}$ is a finite union of sets, there is some $\mathcal{T}_x$ with $\Pr[\mathcal{T}_x]>0$. We define a set $\mathcal{U}\subseteq\mathcal{T}_x$ and find a valuation $v'$ in the following manner:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item If there is some $w\in\mathcal{T}_x$ with $\Pr[w]>0$ (in the case of a distribution with a point mass), define $\mathcal{U}\coloneq \set{w}$ and get $\Pr[\mathcal{U}]>0$. By definition of $\mathcal{T}_x$, there is some valuation $v'>w=\max\mathcal{U}$ such that $\x[\auc{A}]{w}>\x[\auc{A}]{v'}$ and $\trew[\auc{A}]{w}<\trew[\auc{A}]{v'}$.
        \item Else, we can choose some $u\in\mathcal{T}_x$ such that $\mathcal{U}\coloneq\sett{w\in\mathcal{T}_x}{w\leq u}$ has $\Pr[\mathcal{U}]>0$. Since $u\in\mathcal{T}_x$ there is a valuation $v'>u=\max\mathcal{U}$ with $x=\x[\auc{A}]{u}>\x[\auc{A}]{v'}$ and $\trew[\auc{A}]{u}<\trew[\auc{A}]{v'}$, so in particular $\x[\auc{A}]{w}>\x[\auc{A}]{v'}$ for all $w\in\mathcal{U}$. Additionally, since the designer's reward is non-decreasing over valuations in $\mathcal{U}$, the reward function is valuation-independent, and 
        due to Prop.~\ref{prop:decreasing-payments}, the payments for all valuations in $\mathcal{T}_x$ are equal. Therefore also $\trew[\auc{A}]{w}<\trew[\auc{A}]{v'}$ for all $w\in\mathcal{U}$.
    \end{enumerate}
    
    Define $\mathcal{C}\coloneq \set{v'}$. Let $\auc{A}'$ be the auction from Claim~\ref{claim:rev_create_a_tag} over $\mathcal{C}$, with the sequence $\brackets{v_i}$, limit ${v^*}$, allocation ${x^*}$ and $B=\trew[\auc{A}]{v'}$. Clearly ${v^*}=v'$, $v_i=v'$ for all $i$ and ${x^*}=\x[\auc{A}]{v'}$. Due to Claim~\ref{claim:rev_create_a_tag}, for all $w\in\mathcal{V}_1$:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item If $w<v'$, then $\trew[\auc{A}']{w}=\trew[\auc{A}]{w}$ or $\trew[\auc{A}']{w}=B=\trew[\auc{A}]{v'}\geq \trew[\auc{A}]{w}$, where the inequality holds due to $w,v'\in\mathcal{V}_1$.
        \item For all $w\in\mathcal{U}$, since $w<v'$ and $\x[\auc{A}]{w}>\x[\auc{A}]{v'}={x^*}$, then $\trew[\auc{A}']{w}=B=\trew[\auc{A}]{v'}>\trew[\auc{A}]{w}$.
        \item For $w=v'$, it holds that $\trew[\auc{A}']{v'}=B=\trew[\auc{A}]{v'}$.
        \item For $w>v'$, it holds that $\trew[\auc{A}']{w}\geq \trew[\auc{A}]{w}$.
    \end{itemize}

    Putting it together, since $\mathcal{U}\subseteq\mathcal{V}_1$, we have
    \begin{align*}
         \bb{E}[\auc{A}']&=\bb{E}[\trew[\auc{A}']{w}\mid w\in\mathcal{U}]\cdot\Pr[\mathcal{U}]+\bb{E}[\trew[\auc{A}']{w}\mid w\in\mathcal{V}_1\setminus\mathcal{U}]\cdot\Pr\sqbr{\mathcal{V}_1\setminus\mathcal{U}}\\
         &\quad+\bb{E}[\trew[\auc{A}']{w}\mid w\in\mathcal{V}\setminus\mathcal{V}_1]\cdot\Pr[\mathcal{V}\setminus\mathcal{V}_1]\\
        &>\bb{E}[\trew[\auc{A}]{w}\mid w\in\mathcal{U}]\cdot\Pr[\mathcal{U}]+\bb{E}[\trew[\auc{A}]{w}\mid \mathcal{V}_1\setminus\mathcal{U}]\cdot\Pr\sqbr{\mathcal{V}_1\setminus\mathcal{U}}\\
         &\quad+\bb{E}[\trew[\auc{A}]{w}\mid w\in\mathcal{V}\setminus\mathcal{V}_1]\cdot\Pr[\mathcal{V}\setminus\mathcal{V}_1]\\
        &=\bb{E}[\auc{A}'].
    \end{align*}
    The inequality is strict because $\Pr[\mathcal{U}]>0$ and for $w\in\mathcal{U}$ the reward in $\auc{A}'$ is strictly higher than in $\auc{A}$. We also use the fact that for $w\in\mathcal{V}_1\setminus\mathcal{U}$ the reward in $\auc{A}$ does not decrease, and that $\Pr\sqbr{\mathcal{V}\setminus\mathcal{V}_1}=0$.
    We showed $\bb{E}[\auc{A}']>\bb{E}[\auc{A}]$ which is a contradiction to the optimality of $\auc{A}$.

nodes.statement: Let aucA be an optimal and truthful SWACxspace with respect to revenue-like reward, where truthfulness is without loss due to Lemma~. Recall that due to Lemma~, there is a set S of probability measure zero, such that for all w,vinS, if w<v then trew[aucA]wleq trew[aucA]v. Define a new auction aucA' which will be like aucA except for the following modifications: item Let B=bracketsVsetminusScupsetpsi be the bidding set of aucA'. item For any bid vinB, the designer in aucA' will sell x[aucA]v units at a total price of p[aucA]v with uniform payments. Specifically, all filters from aucA were removed. item For bid psi, zero units are allocated with zero payment. Suppose there is an agent w that changed his bid between aucA and aucA'. Observe that the only reasons for an agent to change his bid, are either if winS and he was forced to change his bid, or if he could improve his utility (since for any bid in V, the designer receives the same utility for that bid in aucA and in aucA', this tie-breaking rule will not cause a change in bid). Increasing utility in aucA' is not possible by underbidding, since it was just as possible in aucA and would yield the same utility in aucA' as in aucA. Suppose for contradiction that $\auc{A}$
is a finite-menu SWAC\xspace\ (and as such, truthful)
that is FM-optimal w.r.t.\ the reward function
$g(v,p) = \alpha v + \beta p$,
where  either $\alpha,\beta > 0$ or $\beta<0$ and $\alpha\geq|\beta|$.
This covers positive and negative tradeoff reward that is not welfare-\ or revenue-like (recall that for welfare-\ or revenue-like reward our results are not restricted to FM-optimality).

Let $\mathcal{I}_1,\ldots,\mathcal{I}_k$
be the menu intervals of $\auc{A}$,
and let $x_1,\ldots,x_k$
and $p_1,\dots,p_k$
be the corresponding allocations and total payments, respectively.
Since $\auc{A}$ is not allocation-monotone\xspace\ (which is equivalent to strongly-allocation-monotone\xspace\ in a finite-menu SWAC\xspace), we can define 
\begin{equation*}
    x^\ast\coloneq\max\set{x\in\sqrrange{n}:x\textnormal{ violates monotonicity from the left}},
\end{equation*}
where we say that ``$x$ violates monotonicity from the left'' if there is some agent $w$ with allocation $x$ in $\auc{A}$, and another agent $v>w$ that gets a smaller allocation.

Let $\mathcal{I}_i$ be the \emph{first} interval with $x_i=x^\ast$. By the choice of $\mathcal{I}_i$ it follows that:
\begin{itemize}
    \item All lower intervals have lower allocations:
    for all $j<i$ we have $x_j<x_i$.
    \item The next interval, $I_{i+1}$, does not have a higher allocation: $x_i\geq x_{i+1}$.
\end{itemize}

We construct a new finite-menu SWAC\xspace\ that achieves strictly higher expected reward than $\auc{A}$, contradicting its FM-optimality.
The transformation depends on the relationship between 
$\bb{E}\sqbr{\trew[\auc{A}]{v}\mid v\in\mathcal{I}_i}$,
the actual expected reward from agents in $\mathcal{I}_i$,
and
$\bb{E}\sqbr{\rew[\auc{A}]{v}{\mathcal{I}_{i+1}}\mid v\in\mathcal{I}_i}$, 
the expected reward from agents in $\mathcal{I}_i$ if they were to bid $\mathcal{I}_{i+1}$ in $\auc{A}$.

\paragraph{The case of $\bb{E}\sqbr{\trew[\auc{A}]{v}\mid v\in\mathcal{I}_i}\geq\bb{E}\sqbr{\rew[\auc{A}]{v}{\mathcal{I}_{i+1}}\mid v\in\mathcal{I}_i}$.}


We design a SWAC\xspace $\auc{A}'$ that is identical to $\auc{A}$ except for the following changes:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item We remove interval $\mathcal{I}_{i+1}$,
    and instead extend interval $\mathcal{I}_i$ into $\mathcal{I}_i' = \mathcal{I}_i \cup \mathcal{I}_{i+1}$.
    \item Using filters, we adjust the payment schedule for bids above $\mathcal{I}_{i+1}$ while keeping total payments unchanged, so  that agents in $\mathcal{I}_{i+1}$ \emph{cannot overbid},
    but agents in intervals above $\mathcal{I}_{i+1}$
    do not have to change their bid. Formally, for intervals $\mathcal{I}_j$ where $j>i+1$ rearrange the payment schedule to be as follows:
            \begin{itemize}
                \item The payment for the first unit is $\max\set{t_j,\sfrac{p_j}{x_j}}$ (possible due to Prop.~\ref{prop:finauc_payments_at_least_thresh}).
                \item The payment for subsequent units is divided evenly and sums up, together with the first unit payment, to $p_i$.
            \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}
The intervals below and above intervals $\mathcal{I}_i$ and $\mathcal{I}_{i+1}$ remain unchanged,
$\mathcal{I}_j' = \mathcal{I}_j$ for each $j \notin \set{i, i+1}$.
Intervals below $\mathcal{I}_i$ keep the same allocation and payment schedule, and intervals above $\mathcal{I}_{i+1}$ keep the same allocation but have a modified payment schedule as described above.


Observe that no agent
\emph{outside} $\mathcal{I}_{i+1}$
has an incentive to change their bid in $\auc{A}'$ compared to $\auc{A}$:
no filter was removed and no payment was reduced.
Therefore, agents with valuations outside $\mathcal{I}_{i+1}$ are still truthful in $\auc{A}'$.
On the other hand, agents in $\mathcal{I}_{i+1}$ are \emph{forced} to change their bid.
By design of $\auc{A}'$ they cannot overbid,
so they must switch to a lower interval $\mathcal{I}_j'$
for some $j \leq i$.
In fact, all agents in $\mathcal{I}_{i+1}$
switch to $\mathcal{I}_i'$:
by Prop.~\ref{prop:benefit_swap},
if some agent $v \in \mathcal{I}_{i+1}$
prefers to switch to some lower interval $\mathcal{I}_j'$
where $j < i$,
then 
since that interval has a lower allocation ($x_j < x_i$),
agents from $\mathcal{I}_i$ \emph{also}
prefer $\mathcal{I}_j$ to $\mathcal{I}_i$.
This would also be true in the original auction $\auc{A}$,
contradicting its truthfulness.
Since $\mathcal{I}_{i+1} \subseteq \mathcal{I}_i'$ and agents in $\mathcal{I}_{i+1}$
now bid $\mathcal{I}_i'$,
their bids in $\auc{A}'$ are truthful.

 Thanks to agents in $\mathcal{I}_{i+1}$
 switching their bid to $\mathcal{I}_i'$, 
 the designer's reward strictly increases in $\auc{A}'$ compared to $\auc{A}$, as we prove in either case:
\begin{itemize}
    \item  If $x_i=x_{i+1}$, then due to Prop.~\ref{prop:decreasing-payments} we have $p_i>p_{i+1}$. Together with the assumption $\bb{E}\sqbr{\trew[\auc{A}]{v}\mid v\in\mathcal{I}_i}\geq\bb{E}\sqbr{\rew[\auc{A}]{v}{\mathcal{I}_{i+1}}\mid v\in\mathcal{I}_i}$, which gives $\beta(p_i-p_{i+1})\geq0$, we get $\beta>0$. Therefore:
            \begin{align*}
            \bb{E}\sqbr{\trew[\auc{A}']{v}\medspace | \medspace v\in\mathcal{I}_{i+1}}&=\alpha x_i\bb{E}\sqbr{v\medspace | \medspace v\in\mathcal{I}_{i+1}}+\beta p_i-c(x_i)\\
            &>\alpha x_{i+1}\bb{E}\sqbr{v\medspace | \medspace v\in\mathcal{I}_{i+1}}+\beta p_{i+1}-c(x_{i+1})\\
            &=\bb{E}\sqbr{\trew[\auc{A}]{v}\mid v\in\mathcal{I}_{i+1}}
            \end{align*}
    \item Else, $x_i>x_{i+1}$. In this case, 
 \begin{align*}
    \bb{E}\sqbr{\auc{A}'}-\bb{E}\sqbr{\auc{A}}&=\bb{E}\sqbr{\rew[\auc{A}']{v}{\mathcal{I}_i'}\medspace | \medspace v\in\mathcal{I}_{i+1}}-\bb{E}\sqbr{\rew[\auc{A}]{v}{\mathcal{I}_{i+1}}\medspace | \medspace v\in\mathcal{I}_{i+1}}\\
    &=\alpha(x_i-x_{i+1})\bb{E}\sqbr{v\medspace | \medspace v\in\mathcal{I}_{i+1}}+\beta(p_i-p_{i+1})-c(x_i)+c(x_{i+1})\\
    &>\alpha(x_i-x_{i+1})\bb{E}\sqbr{v\medspace | \medspace v\in\mathcal{I}_{i}}+\beta(p_i-p_{i+1})-c(x_i)+c(x_{i+1})\\
    &=\bb{E}\sqbr{\trew[\auc{A}]{v}\mid v\in\mathcal{I}_i}-\bb{E}\sqbr{\rew[\auc{A}]{v}{\mathcal{I}_{i+1}}\mid v\in\mathcal{I}_i}\geq0.
\end{align*}
The first inequality is due to
the fact that $x_i>x_{i+1}$ (allocation-monotonicity is violated)
and $\mathcal{I}_{i+1}$ contains only valuations greater than $\mathcal{I}_i$;
the second is our assumption in this case.
\end{itemize}

 
This shows that $\auc{A}'$ is a finite-menu SWAC\xspace that achieves higher expected reward than $\auc{A}$,
contradicting the FM-optimality of $\auc{A}$.

\paragraph{The case of $\bb{E}\sqbr{\trew[\auc{A}]{v}\mid v\in\mathcal{I}_i}<\bb{E}\sqbr{\rew[\auc{A}]{v}{\mathcal{I}_{i+1}}\mid v\in\mathcal{I}_i}$.}
Design a new finite-menu SWAC\xspace\ $\auc{A}'$ that differs from $\auc{A}$ in the following manner:
        \begin{itemize}
            \item Bid $\mathcal{I}_i$ is removed, and instead we extend interval $\mathcal{I}_{i+1}$ into $\mathcal{I}_{i+1}'=\mathcal{I}_i\cup\mathcal{I}_{i+1}$.
            \item The filter on bid $\mathcal{I}_{i+1}$ is lowered to $t_i$ (possible due to Prop.~\ref{prop:un_monotonicity_means_filter}).
        \end{itemize}
        Clearly agents not in $\mathcal{I}_i$ do not change their bid, and are truthful in $\auc{A}'$. Agents in $\mathcal{I}_i$ will now bid $\mathcal{I}_{i+1}'$ since the filter was lowered and due to Prop.~\ref{prop:un_monotonicity_means_filter}. Therefore 
        \begin{align*}
            \bb{E}\sqbr{\trew[\auc{A}']{v}\medspace | \medspace v\in\mathcal{I}_i}=\bb{E}\sqbr{\rew[\auc{A}]{v}{\mathcal{I}_{i+1}}\mid v\in\mathcal{I}_i}>\bb{E}\sqbr{\trew[\auc{A}]{v}\mid v\in\mathcal{I}_i}.
        \end{align*}

    We showed that also in this case, $\bb{E}\sqbr{\auc{A}'}>\bb{E}\sqbr{\auc{A}}$, which is a contradiction to the FM-optimality of $\auc{A}$.

Let $g(v,p)=v- p$ be the reward function consumer surplus, and
    let $\auc{A}$ be an optimal SWAC\xspace with respect to $g$ and some cost function $c$.
    Suppose, for contradiction, that $\auc{A}$ is not allocation-monotone\xspace.
    We use the following terminology an notation in this proof: If there are valuations $w<v$ such that $\x{w}>\x{v}$ we say that $w$ violates monotonicity \emph{from the left} (with respect to $v$) and $v$ violates monotonicity \emph{from the right} (with respect to $w$). For each $v\in\mathcal{V}$ we define the set $\mathcal{S}_v\coloneq\sett{u\in\mathcal{V}}{u<v\textnormal{ and }\x{u}>\x{v}}$  to be all the valuations that violate monotonicity from the left with respect to $v$.
    
    The idea behind the proof is to construct a new auction $\auc{A}'$ based on $\auc{A}$. We find a valuation ${v^*}$ that violates monotonicity from the right with respect to a set $\mathcal{U}$ that has positive probability. We use Prop.~\ref{prop:un_monotonicity_means_filter} to show that if we reduce the filter on bid ${v^*}$, it results in all the bidders of $\mathcal{U}$ changing their bid to ${v^*}$ due to an increase in utility. Our reward function increases with the agents' utility, and the new allocation for agents in $\mathcal{U}$ is lower than their original allocation (meaning it has a lower cost) the designer's reward from all agents in $\mathcal{U}$ strictly increases. If we show that no other agent changes their bid, we reach a contradiction to the optimality of $\auc{A}$.
    
    We now give the details and prove the above formally. 
    For each allocation $x\in\sqrrange{n}$ we define the set of valuations $\mathcal{S}_x$ as the set of valuations that violate allocation-monotonicity from the left with respect to some valuation with allocation $x$. Formally, 
    $$\mathcal{S}_x\coloneq\sett{v\in\mathcal{V}}{\exists u\in\mathcal{V}\textnormal{ s.t. }v<u\textnormal{ and }\x{v}>\x{u}=x}.$$

    If for each $x$ the set $\mathcal{S}_x$ would be of probability zero, then the set 
    $${\mathcal{S}\coloneq\bigcup_{x\in\sqrrange{n}}\mathcal{S}_x}=\sett{v\in\mathcal{V}}{\exists u\in\mathcal{V}\textnormal{ s.t. }v<u\textnormal{ and }\x{v}>\x{u}}$$
    would also be of probability zero, which would be a contradiction to the fact that $\auc{A}$ is \emph{not} allocation-monotone\xspace. Thus we can define 
    \begin{align*}
        &{x^*}\coloneq\min\sett{x\in\sqrrange{n}}{\Pr[\mathcal{S}_x]>0}.
    \end{align*}
    Since we are dealing with a continuous distribution, there is some ${v^*}$ with $\x{{v^*}}={x^*}$ such that ${\Pr[\mathcal{S}_{{v^*}}]>0}$.
    Define
    \begin{align*}
        &w\coloneq\sup\sett{v\in\mathcal{V}}{v<{v^*}\textnormal{ and }\x{v}<{x^*}}.
    \end{align*}
    
    Define a new auction $\auc{A}'$ that is based on $\auc{A}$, but for bid ${v^*}$ the filter is reduced to $\max\set{w,\frac{\p{{v^*}}}{\x{{v^*}}}}$. Note that this change does not affect the agents with valuations below $w$, since the filter is not lowered enough. Additionally it does not affect valuations from ${v^*}$ or higher, since the total payment does not change. Thus the only agents who may bid non-truthfully in $\auc{A}'$ are those in $[w,{v^*})$. Let $v\in[w,{v^*})$:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item If $\x[\auc{A}]{v}>{x^*}=\x[\auc{A}]{{v^*}}$ due to Prop.~\ref{prop:un_monotonicity_means_filter} we know that agent $v$ strictly increases their utility by bidding ${v^*}$, and this is possible in $\auc{A}'$ since the filter is lowered enough, thus $v$ will bid ${v^*}$ in $\auc{A}'$. Additionally since $\x[\auc{A}]{v}>{x^*}=\xhat[\auc{A}']{v}$ we have $c\brackets{\xhat[\auc{A}']{v}}\leq c\brackets{\xhat[\auc{A}]{v}}$, thus:
        \begin{align*}
            \trew[\auc{A}']{v}-\trew[\auc{A}]{v}&=\util[\auc{A}']{v}{{v^*}}-\util[\auc{A}]{v}{v}+c\brackets{\xhat[\auc{A}]{v}}-c\brackets{\xhat[\auc{A}']{v}}>0.
        \end{align*}
        This shows that the designer's reward from $v$ is strictly larger in $\auc{A}'$ than in $\auc{A}$.
        \item If $\x[\auc{A}]{v}={x^*}$ and $v$ bids ${v^*}$ in $\auc{A}'$, this also strictly increases the designer's reward as in the above case, since the agent's utility strictly increases and the cost does not change.
        \item Else, $\x[\auc{A}]{v}<{x^*}$. But this is only possible for $v=w$ by definition of $w$. Since the distribution is continuous, $\Pr[w]=0$, so even if bidder $w$ yields less reward in $\auc{A}'$ than in $\auc{A}$, this does not affect the expected utility of $\auc{A}'$.
    \end{enumerate}
    
    We showed that all agents in $\mathcal{U}\coloneq\mathcal{S}_{{v^*}}\cap[w,{v^*})$ yield strictly larger utility for the designer in $\auc{A}'$ relative to $\auc{A}$, and there is no other change in terms of expected reward for the designer. We want to show that $\Pr[\mathcal{U}]>0$ and we do this by contradiction. Suppose $\Pr[\mathcal{U}]=0$. In this case $\Pr[\mathcal{S}_{{v^*}}\cap[0,w)]>0$. Once again due to the continuity of the distribution, we can find a valuation $u\leq w$ with $\x[\auc{A}]{u}<{x^*}$ and  $\Pr[\mathcal{S}_{{v^*}}\cap[0,u)]>0$.
    By definition of $\mathcal{S}_u$, $S_{{v^*}}$ and since $\x[\auc{A}]{u}<\x[\auc{A}]{{v^*}}$  it holds that $\mathcal{S}_{{v^*}}\cap[0,u)\subseteq\mathcal{S}_u$, so also $\Pr[\mathcal{S}_u]>0$. This is a contradiction to the choice of ${x^*}$, so we deduce that $\Pr[\mathcal{U}]>0$.

    Putting it all together, we show that the expected reward of $\auc{A}'$ is larger than that of $\auc{A}$:
    \begin{align*}
        \bb{E}\sqbr{\auc{A}'}&=\bb{E}\sqbr{\trew[\auc{A}']{v}\mid v\notin\mathcal{U}}\cdot\Pr[v\notin\mathcal{U}]+\bb{E}\sqbr{\rew[\auc{A}']{v}{{v^*}}\mid v\in\mathcal{U}}\cdot\Pr[v\in\mathcal{U}]\\
        &>\bb{E}\sqbr{\trew[\auc{A}]{v}\mid v\notin\mathcal{U}}\cdot\Pr[v\notin\mathcal{U}]+\bb{E}\sqbr{\trew[\auc{A}]{v}\mid v\in\mathcal{U}}\cdot\Pr[v\in\mathcal{U}]
        =\bb{E}\sqbr{\auc{A}}
    \end{align*}

    This result is in contradiction to the optimality of $\auc{A}$, completing the proof.

Let $\auc{A}$ be a truthful optimal SWAC\xspace with respect to consumer surplus matching the conditions of the Lemma. Due to Lemma~\ref{lemma:consumer-surplus-amono} we know that $\auc{A}$ is allocation-monotone\xspace, thus there exists a set $\mathcal{S}$ with $\Pr[\mathcal{S}]=0$ such that for all $u,v\in\mathcal{V}\setminus\mathcal{S}$ it holds that $\x[\auc{A}]{u}\leq\x[\auc{A}]{v}$. Define an auction $\auc{A}'$ with a bidding set $\mathcal{B}\coloneq\brackets{\mathcal{V}\setminus\mathcal{S}}\cup\set{\emptyset}$. For bids in $\mathcal{V}\setminus\mathcal{S}$ agents get in $\auc{A}'$ the exact same conditions as in $\auc{A}$ (allocation and payment schedule), while an agent bidding $\emptyset$ gets nothing and pays nothing.

    Clearly all agents in $\mathcal{V}\setminus\mathcal{S}$ will still bid truthfully in $\auc{A}'$, and the change in reward from agents in $\mathcal{S}$ has no affect on the total expected reward of $\auc{A}'$ when compared to $\auc{A}$, due to the fact that $\Pr[\mathcal{S}]=0$. Additionally $\auc{A}'$ is stagewise-IR\xspace\ since agents have the option of bidding $\emptyset$ for a utility of zero.

    Finally, it remains to show that $\auc{A}'$ is strongly-allocation-monotone\xspace. Let $u,v\in\mathcal{V}$ and suppose that $\xhat[\auc{A}']{u}>\xhat[\auc{A}']{v}$. Due to Prop.~\ref{prop:un_monotonicity_means_filter}, neither agent bids $\emptyset$ in $\auc{A}'$. Thus by the design of $\auc{A}'$, agent $w$ bids a value higher than that of $v$'s bid in $\auc{A}'$, but this means that agent $w$ \emph{is} able to make the same bid as $w$ in $\auc{A}'$, in contradiction to Prop.~\ref{prop:un_monotonicity_means_filter}. Therefore $\auc{A}'$ is strongly-allocation-monotone\xspace\ and this completes the proof.

nodes.statement: Let aucA be an FM-optimal SWACxspace w.r.t. a positive tradeoff reward g(v,p)=alpha v+beta p and cost function c. Denote its intervals in increasing order by I_1,dots,I_k and their respective allocations with x_1leqdotsleq x_k. Due to Lemma~, aucA is strongly-allocation-monotonexspace. Suppose, for contradiction, that aucA is not reward-monotonexspace. In this case there is some interval I_i such that bbEsqbrtrew[aucA]vmedspace | medspace vinI_i>bbEsqbrtrew[aucA]vmedspace | medspace vinI_i. Denoting v_j=bbEsqbrvinI_j for all jin[k] and expanding on the definition of reward gives us alpha x_iv_i+beta p_i-c(x_i)>alpha x_i+1 v_i+1+beta p_i+1-c(x_i+1). Design a new SWACxspace aucA' that is based on aucA but for these differences: item We remove interval I_i+1, and instead extend interval I_i into I_i' = I_i cup I_i+1. item We adjust the payment schedule for bids above I_i+1 while keeping total payments unchanged, so that agents in I_i+1 cannot overbid (this is feasible due to Prop.~). The intervals below and above intervals I_i and I_i+1 remain unchanged, I_j' = I_j for each j notin seti, i+1. Intervals below I_i keep the same allocation and payment schedule, and intervals above I_i+1 keep the same allocation but have a possibly modified payment schedule. Observe that no agent outside I_i+1 has an incentive to change their bid in aucA' compared to aucA: no filter was removed and no payment was reduced. Therefore, agents with valuations outside I_i+1 are truthful in aucA'. On the other hand, agents in I_i+1 are forced to change their bid. By design of aucA' they cannot overbid, so they must switch to a lower interval I_j' for some j leq i. In fact, we show that agents in I_i+1 must switch to I_i': suppose they switch to some lower interval I_j' = I_j where j < i. By choice of I_i we have x_j leq x_i. If x_j=x_i then by Prop.~ agents in I_i+1 would prefer to bid I_i' in aucA'. Else, x_j<x_i. However, if agents from I_i+1 prefer to bid I_j' = I_j over I_i', this means agents from I_i also prefer I_j' to I_i', as their utility would be improved due to Prop.~. Consequently, since I_i and I_j are equivalent to I_i' to I_j', we obtain a contradiction to the truthfulness of agents in I_i in the original auction aucA. Thanks to agents in I_i+1 switching their bid, the designer's reward strictly increases in aucA' compared to aucA: bbE[aucA']-bbE[aucA]&=bbEsqbrtrew[aucA']vmedspace | medspace vinI_i+1-bbEsqbrtrew[aucA]vmedspace | medspace vinI_i+1\\ &=alpha v_i+1x_i+beta p_i-c(x_i)-alpha v_i+1x_i+1-beta p_i+1+c(x_i+1)\\ &>alpha v_i+1x_i+beta p_i+1-c(x_i+1)-alpha x_iv_i-beta p_i+1+c(x_i+1)\\ &=alpha x_i (v_i+1-v_i)geq 0. The first inequality is due to our assumption, as seen in Eq.~. Since aucA' is a finite-menu SWACxspace we reach a contradiction to the FM-optimality of aucA.

Let $\auc{A}$ be an FM-optimal SWAC\xspace w.r.t. a positive tradeoff reward $g(v,p)=\alpha v+\beta p$ and cost function $c$. Denote its intervals in increasing order by $\mathcal{I}_1,\dots,\mathcal{I}_k$ and their respective allocations with $x_1\leq\dots\leq x_k$. Due to Lemma~\ref{lemma:pos-neg-tradeoff-samono}, $\auc{A}$ is strongly-allocation-monotone\xspace. Suppose, for contradiction, that $\auc{A}$ is not reward-monotone\xspace. In this case there is some interval $\mathcal{I}_i$ such that
    \begin{equation}
        \bb{E}\sqbr{\trew[\auc{A}]{v}\medspace | \medspace v\in\mathcal{I}_i}>\bb{E}\sqbr{\trew[\auc{A}]{v}\medspace | \medspace v\in\mathcal{I}_i}.
    \end{equation}
    Denoting $v_j=\bb{E}\sqbr{v\in\mathcal{I}_j}$ for all $j\in[k]$ and expanding on the definition of reward gives us
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:pos-tradeoff-rmono}
        \alpha x_iv_i+\beta p_i-c(x_i)>\alpha x_{i+1} v_{i+1}+\beta p_{i+1}-c(x_{i+1}).
    \end{equation}
    Design a new SWAC\xspace $\auc{A}'$ that is based on $\auc{A}$ but for these differences:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item We remove interval $\mathcal{I}_{i+1}$,
        and instead extend interval $\mathcal{I}_i$ into $\mathcal{I}_i' = \mathcal{I}_i \cup \mathcal{I}_{i+1}$.
        \item We adjust the payment schedule for bids above $\mathcal{I}_{i+1}$ while keeping total payments unchanged, so that agents in $\mathcal{I}_{i+1}$ \emph{cannot} overbid (this is feasible due to Prop.~\ref{prop:finauc_payments_at_least_thresh}).
    \end{enumerate}
    The intervals below and above intervals $\mathcal{I}_i$ and $\mathcal{I}_{i+1}$ remain unchanged,
    $\mathcal{I}_j' = \mathcal{I}_j$ for each $j \notin \set{i, i+1}$.
    Intervals below $\mathcal{I}_i$ keep the same allocation and payment schedule, and intervals above $\mathcal{I}_{i+1}$ keep the same allocation but have a possibly modified payment schedule.
    Observe that no agent
\emph{outside} $\mathcal{I}_{i+1}$
has an incentive to change their bid in $\auc{A}'$ compared to $\auc{A}$:
no filter was removed and no payment was reduced.

Therefore, agents with valuations outside $\mathcal{I}_{i+1}$ are truthful in $\auc{A}'$.
On the other hand, agents in $\mathcal{I}_{i+1}$ are \emph{forced} to change their bid.
By design of $\auc{A}'$ they cannot overbid,
so they must switch to a lower interval $\mathcal{I}_j'$
for some $j \leq i$.
In fact, we show that agents in $\mathcal{I}_{i+1}$
must switch to $\mathcal{I}_i'$:
suppose they switch to some lower interval $\mathcal{I}_j' = \mathcal{I}_j$
where $j < i$.
By choice of $\mathcal{I}_i$ we have $x_j \leq x_i$. 

If $x_j=x_i$ then by Prop.~\ref{prop:decreasing-payments} agents in $\mathcal{I}_{i+1}$ would prefer to bid $\mathcal{I}_i'$ in $\auc{A}'$. 

Else, $x_j<x_i$.
However,
if 
agents from $\mathcal{I}_{i+1}$ prefer to bid $\mathcal{I}_j' = \mathcal{I}_j$
over $\mathcal{I}_i'$,
this means agents from $\mathcal{I}_i$ \emph{also}
prefer $\mathcal{I}_j'$ to $\mathcal{I}_i'$,
as their utility would be improved due to Prop.~\ref{prop:benefit_swap}.
Consequently, since $\mathcal{I}_i$ and $\mathcal{I}_j$ are equivalent to $\mathcal{I}_i'$ to $\mathcal{I}_j'$,
we obtain a contradiction to the truthfulness of agents in $\mathcal{I}_i$ in the original auction $\auc{A}$.
 Thanks to agents in $\mathcal{I}_{i+1}$
 switching their bid, 
 the designer's reward strictly increases in $\auc{A}'$ compared to $\auc{A}$:
\begin{align*}
    \bb{E}[\auc{A}']-\bb{E}[\auc{A}]&=\bb{E}\sqbr{\trew[\auc{A}']{v}\medspace | \medspace v\in\mathcal{I}_{i+1}}-\bb{E}\sqbr{\trew[\auc{A}]{v}\medspace | \medspace v\in\mathcal{I}_{i+1}}\\
    &=\alpha v_{i+1}x_i+\beta p_i-c(x_i)-\alpha v_{i+1}x_{i+1}-\beta p_{i+1}+c(x_{i+1})\\
    &>\alpha v_{i+1}x_i+\beta p_{i+1}-c(x_{i+1})-\alpha x_iv_i-\beta p_{i+1}+c(x_{i+1})\\
    &=\alpha x_i (v_{i+1}-v_i)\geq 0.
\end{align*}
The first inequality is due to our assumption, as seen in Eq.~\ref{eq:pos-tradeoff-rmono}.
Since $\auc{A}'$ is a finite-menu SWAC\xspace we reach a contradiction to the FM-optimality of $\auc{A}$.

nodes.statement: Let g and c be function per the claim, and let aucA be an FM-optimal SWACxspace. Due to Lemma~, aucA is strongly-allocation-monotonexspace. We denote the intervals of aucA by I_1,dots,I_k with allocations x_1,dots,x_k, thresholds t_1,dots,t_k and total payments p_1,dots,p_k. Consider an interval I_i in aucA and the following interval I_i+1. If p_i+1>p_i+(x_i+1-x_i)t_i+1, for some vinI_i+1 we have utilvI_i=x_iv-p_i>x_iv-p_i+1+x_i+1t_i+1-x_it_i+1=utilvI_i+1+x_i(v-t_i+1)geq utilvI_i+1, which is a contradiction to the truthfulness of aucA, giving us p_i+1leq p_i+(x_i+1-x_i)t_i+1. We design a stagewise auction aucA' over the same intervals as aucA, and set the payments recursively as p_i+1'=p_i'+(x_i+1-x_i)t_i+1, where we define p_0'=0 and x_0=0 (p_i' is the payment in aucA' for interval I_i). The payment schedule is fixed-ratexspace. Observe that this is exactly the unique payment rule of Myerson that guarantees optimality for a monotone allocation rule. Since in a fixed-ratexspace SWACxspace there are no filters, Myerson's proof applies as is, and aucA' is truthful and a finite-menu SWACxspace. Given Eq.~, and due to the optimality of aucA, we have that p_i+1= p_i+(x_i+1-x_i)t_i+1 exactly.

nodes.statement: To begin with, we explain the precomputations of Algorithm~. For each horizon h, the algorithm returns a set of disjoint consecutive intervals over the ironed virtual value space, such that there is a single interval for each allocation in set1,dots,h. Each interval is of type textscInterval, that contains fields left,\ right,\ alloc and pay. We use aucA_h to denote Algorithm~ at horizon h, for each hinset0,1,dots,n. We will prove by induction on h that (1) aucA_h is optimal, among all fixed-ratexspace SWACsxspace, with respect to the over-time cost function, and (2) that R[h] is exactly R_h, the expected reward from the final h horizons. The horizon of h=0 is trivial, so we assume that aucA_i is optimal (among fixed-ratexspace\ SWACsxspace) for i<h and prove for h>0. Consider an agent vinV. Let J be the interval in intervals[h] that includes qcoloneqBarvarphi_h(v), and denote x=J.alloc. We will show that x maximizes the expression qy-c_n,g^boldsymbolD(y) over all yinsqrrangen, and chooses the smallest maximizing y. By definition of the over-time cost function, this is equivalent to maximizing qy+R_h-maxsety,1. item If x=0, since R_h is always nonnegative and monotone non-decreasing, we have that q<0, because q wasn't even in an interval with allocation 1. Therefore 0cdot q+R_h-1geq yq+R_h-y for any ygeq1. item If x=1, by the algorithm's definition 0leq qleq fracR[h-1]-R[h-y]y-x for y>x. It follows that: item Since c(0)=c(1) and 0leq q, clearly q+R_h-1geq 0+R_h-maxset0,1. item By the induction hypothesis, qleq fracR_h-1-R_h-yy-x for all y>x, meaning yq+R_h-yleq xq+R_h-x for all y>1. item Else, xgeq2. By the algorithm's definition, q was allocated x-1geq 1 units at horizon h-1, and thus (x-1)q+R_h-1-(x-1)geq y'q+R_h-1-y' for all y'insqrrangeh-1. Setting y=y'+1 it follows that xq+R_h-xgeq yq+R_h-y for all yinpsqrrangeh. Additionally since q is greater than the left of the interval, and all of the left fields are at least 0 by the algorithm's definition, we have qgeq0 and therefore xq+R_h-xgeq q+R_h-1geq R_h-1. We finished showing that x maximizes the wanted expression. The fact that the allocation chosen is the smallest maximizing one follows from the design of the algorithm, that starts an interval only after the end of the intervals for smaller allocations. We will show that the allocation rule alloc we get from Algorithm~ is monotone non-decreasing, using the fact that it maximizes Barvarphi_h(v)xv-cbracketsxv. Let w<v be valuations and suppose, for contradiction, that xw>xv. Due to the maximization of alloc and by the fact that the smallest allocation is chosen, &Barvarphi_h(w)xw-cbracketsxw>Barvarphi_h(w)xv-cbracketsxv,textnormal and\\ &Barvarphi_h(v)xv-cbracketsxvgeqBarvarphi_h(v)xw-cbracketsxw. Combining the above inequalities we get Barvarphi_h(w)bracketsxw-xv>Barvarphi_h(v)bracketsxw-xv. Since Barvarphi_h(cdot) is monotone non-decreasing, this yields Barvarphi_h(w)bracketsxw-xv>Barvarphi_h(w)bracketsxw-xv which is a contradiction. Thus, alloc is monotone non-decreasing. Due to Observation~, in a fixed-ratexspace SWACxspace the allocation determines the payment schedules, and its allocation rule is monotone. Additionally, as we showed in Proposition~, theta_h is a fixed-ratexspace-optimal virtual value. Thus, together with Lemma~, aucA_h is optimal among all SWACsxspace with monotone allocation rules, and specifically, among all fixed-ratexspace SWACsxspace. Additionally, based on the induction hypothesis and since we showed that xBarvarphi(v)+R_h-x is maximized, also R[h] is exactly the expected reward from horizon h. Finally, we conclude that aucA_h is an optimal SWACxspace\ for horizon h, among fixed-ratexspace\ SWACsxspace. This completes the proof by induction.

To begin with, we explain the precomputations of Algorithm~\ref{alg:cal-intervals}. For each horizon $h$, the algorithm returns a set of disjoint consecutive intervals over the ironed virtual value space, such that there is a single interval for each allocation in $\set{1,\dots,h}$.
Each interval is of type $\textsc{Interval}$, that contains fields $left,\ right,\ alloc$ and $pay$.


    We use $\auc{A}_h$ to denote Algorithm~\ref{alg:fr-rental} at horizon $h$, for each $h\in\set{0,1,\dots,n}$. We will prove by induction on $h$ that (1) $\auc{A}_h$ is optimal, among all fixed-rate\xspace SWACs\xspace, with respect to the over-time cost function, and (2) that $R[h]$ is exactly $R_h$, the expected reward from the final $h$ horizons.

    The horizon of $h=0$ is trivial, so we assume that $\auc{A}_i$ is  optimal (among fixed-rate\xspace\ SWACs\xspace) for $i<h$ and prove for $h>0$. Consider an agent $v\in\mathcal{V}$. Let $J$ be the interval in $intervals[h]$ that includes $q\coloneq\Bar{\varphi}_h(v)$, and denote $x=J.alloc$. We will show that $x$ maximizes the expression $qy-c_{n,g}^{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{D}}}(y)$ over all $y\in\sqrrange{n}$, and chooses the \emph{smallest} maximizing $y$. By definition of the over-time cost function, this is equivalent to maximizing $qy+R_{h-\max\set{y,1}}$. 

    \begin{itemize}
        \item If $x=0$, since $R_{h}$ is always nonnegative and monotone non-decreasing, we have that $q<0$, because $q$ wasn't even in an interval with allocation $1$. Therefore $0\cdot q+R_{h-1}\geq yq+R_{h-y}$ for any $y\geq1$.
        \item If $x=1$, by the algorithm's definition $0\leq q\leq \frac{R[h-1]-R[h-y]}{y-x}$ for $y>x$. It follows that:
            \begin{itemize}
                \item Since $c(0)=c(1)$ and $0\leq q$, clearly $q+R_{h-1}\geq 0+R_{h-\max\set{0,1}}$.
                \item By the induction hypothesis, $q\leq \frac{R_{h-1}-R_{h-y}}{y-x}$ for all $y>x$, meaning $yq+R_{h-y}\leq xq+R_{h-x}$ for all $y>1$.
            \end{itemize}
        \item Else, $x\geq2$. By the algorithm's definition, $q$ was allocated $x-1\geq 1$ units at horizon $h-1$, and thus $(x-1)q+R_{h-1-(x-1)}\geq y'q+R_{h-1-y'}$ for all $y'\in\sqrrange{h-1}$.
        Setting $y=y'+1$ it follows that $xq+R_{h-x}\geq yq+R_{h-y}$ for all $y\in\psqrrange{h}$. Additionally since $q$ is greater than the $left$ of the interval, and all of the $left$ fields are at least $0$ by the algorithm's definition, we have $q\geq0$ and therefore $xq+R_{h-x}\geq q+R_{h-1}\geq R_{h-1}$.
    \end{itemize}

    We finished showing that $x$ maximizes the wanted expression. The fact that the allocation chosen is the smallest maximizing one follows from the design of the algorithm, that 
    starts an interval only after the end of the intervals for smaller allocations.
    We will show that the allocation rule $\alloc$ we get from Algorithm~\ref{alg:cal-intervals} is monotone non-decreasing, using the fact that it maximizes $\Bar{\varphi}_h(v)\x{v}-c\brackets{\x{v}}$. Let $w<v$ be valuations and suppose, for contradiction, that $\x{w}>\x{v}$. Due to the maximization of $\alloc$ and by the fact that the smallest allocation is chosen,
    \begin{align*}
    &\Bar{\varphi}_h(w)\x{w}-c\brackets{\x{w}}>\Bar{\varphi}_h(w)\x{v}-c\brackets{\x{v}},\textnormal{ and}\\
        &\Bar{\varphi}_h(v)\x{v}-c\brackets{\x{v}}\geq\Bar{\varphi}_h(v)\x{w}-c\brackets{\x{w}}.
    \end{align*}

Thus, $\alloc$ is monotone non-decreasing.   

    Due to Observation~\ref{ob:fr-means-myerson}, in a fixed-rate\xspace SWAC\xspace the allocation determines the payment schedules, and its allocation rule is monotone. Additionally, as we showed in Proposition~\ref{prop:generelized-virv}, $\theta_h$ is a fixed-rate\xspace-optimal virtual value.
    Thus, together with Lemma~\ref{lemma:irn-maximizer-maximizes-expected}, $\auc{A}_h$ is optimal among all SWACs\xspace with monotone allocation rules, and specifically, among all fixed-rate\xspace SWACs\xspace.
    
    Additionally, based on the induction hypothesis and since we showed that $x\Bar{\varphi}(v)+R_{h-x}$ is maximized, also $R[h]$ is exactly the expected reward from horizon $h$. Finally, we conclude that $\auc{A}_h$ is an optimal SWAC\xspace\ for horizon $h$, among fixed-rate\xspace\ SWACs\xspace. 
    
     This completes the proof by induction.

Since in $\auc{A}'$ they can receive 1 unit for free instead of 1 unit at the cost of $t$, they will bid below $t$ in $\auc{A}'$. In contrast, an agent $v\geq s$ will not change their bid in $\auc{A}'$, since
    \begin{align*}
        \util[\auc{A}']{v}{v}=\x{v}v-\p{v}\geq 2v-v=v
    \end{align*}
    and $v$ is their utility from bidding below $t$, which is the only difference between $\auc{A}$ and $\auc{A}'$.

Additionally, when we write optimal in this proof, we mean FM-optimal, unless the reward is consumer surplus, in which case we are really referring to global optimality. Assume that the reward takes the form of g(v,p)=alpha v-beta p. First, observe that truthfulness follows from Lemma~. We move on to show, by induction on n, that: item The allocation from Algorithm~, which we denote alloc, maximizes Barvarphi_n(v)xv-cbracketsxv pointwise, and item Algorithm~ for horizon n is optimal. item The value R[n] returned from Algorithm~ is equal to the expected reward from horizon n, which we denote R_n. For n=1 all claims are easy to see (when there is a single unit, for negative tradeoff it is clearly optimal to give the unit for free to any agent, resulting in an expected reward of bbE[alpha v]). Now assume correctness up to n-1 and prove for ngeq2. The first step is to show that an allocation of 0 is never required for optimality: by definition of the virtual value for revenue, varphi_g,n(v) = alpha v-fracbetan-1bracketsv-frac1-F(v)f(v) geq beta vbrackets1-frac1n-1+betafrac1-F(v)f(v)(n-1) geq 0 . By definition of the ironing process (Def.~), also Barvarphi_n(v)geq0. Since c_n(1)=c_n(0), Barvarphi_ncdot0 - c_nbrackets0leq Barvarphi_ncdot 1 - c_nbrackets1, and hence an optimal allocation can always allocate at least one day to any agent. This allows us to focus on strictly positive allocations, and prove pointwise optimality by showing that for any valuation v in V, our allocation rule is no worse than any other positive allocation x geq 1: Barvarphi_n(v)cdotxv-c_n(xv)geqBarvarphi_n(v)cdot x-c_n(x). Suppose Barvarphi_n(v)<R_n-1/(n-1) , so that xv = 1. Then for any x geq 1, Barvarphi_n(v)x-c_n(x)&=Barvarphi_n(v)+(x-1)Barvarphi_n(v)-R_n-1+R_n-x < Barvarphi_n(v)+fracx-1n-1R_n-1-R_n-1+R_n-x \\ &= Barvarphi_n(v)+(n-x)bracketsfracR_n-xn-x-fracR_n-1n-1. We now rely on an interesting (and intuitive) fact, which we prove in Lemma~: if a monotone allocation rule of one or all, as in Algorithm~ is w.l.o.g., then the expected average daily reward from a rental game with negative tradeoff reward is non-decreasing in the horizon; that is, if n > m then R_n/ngeq R_m/m. We can apply Lemma~ thanks to our induction hypothesis, which tells us that Algorithm~ is indeed optimal. Therefore, Barvarphi_n(v)+(n-x)bracketsfracR_n-xn-x-fracR_n-1n-1 leq Barvarphi_n(v) = Barvarphi_n(v) cdot 1 -c_n(1). Now suppose Barvarphi_n(v)geq R_n-1/(n-1), so that xv=n. Then for any xgeq 1, nBarvarphi_n(v)-c(n)&=xBarvarphi_n(v)-R_n-1+R_n-x+(n-x)Barvarphi_n(v)-R_n-x\\ &geq xBarvarphi_n(v)-R_n-1+R_n-x+(n-x)bracketsfracR_n-1n-1-fracR_n-xn-x\\ &geq xBarvarphi_n(v)-R_n-1 Here too the last inequality is due to Lemma~ and Item~ from the induction hypothesis. This completes the induction proof for Item~ for n. By Lemma~ (and Lemma~ for consumer surplus), allocation monotonicity is w.l.o.g. for g, meaning that there is an optimal SWACxspace aucA^ast with a monotone allocation rule x[aucA^ast]cdot. Since alloc is pointwise maximizing, we can apply Lemma~, telling us that bbEsqbrvarphi_n(v)xv-cbracketsxv is maximized among all monotone non-decreasing allocation rules. Specifically, bbEsqbrvarphi_n(v)x[aucA^ast]v-cbracketsx[aucA^ast]vleqbbEsqbrvarphi_n(v)xv-cbracketsxv. Combining Equation~ with Lemma~ gives us: bbEsqbrtrew[aucA^ast]vleqbbEsqbrvarphi_n(v)xv-cbracketsxv. Denote Algorithm~ at horizon n by aucA_n. Observe that since aucA_n is a one-or-all threshold auction, the payment charged is exactly equal to 1/(n-1) of the Myerson payment: if v is allocated one unit, its threshold payment and the Myerson payment are both zero; if v is greater than the threshold t and the agent is allocated n units, the threshold payment is t while the Myerson payment is (n-1)cdot t. Therefore, if we denote the total payment rule of aucA_n by pcdot and the Myerson payment rule by p[My]cdot, bbEsqbrtrew[aucA_n]v&=bbEsqbralphaxv v -betapv-cbracketsxv \\ &=bbEsqbralphaxv v -fracbetan-1p[My]v-cbracketsxv =bbEsqbralphaxv v -betafracvarphi(v)xvn-1-cbracketsxv \\ & =bbEsqbrxvgbracketsv,fracvarphi(v)n-1-cbracketsxv =bbEsqbrvarphi_n(v)xv-cbracketsxv. Combining this equality with Equation~, bbEsqbrtrew[aucA_n]vgeqbbEsqbrtrew[aucA^ast]v, completing the proof of the optimality of aucA_n, which is Item~ in the induction claim. Once we showed aucA_n is optimal, it is clear that R[n]=R_n, as it calculates the expected reward from an optimal SWACxspace.

nodes.statement: We prove this claim by induction on n. For n=1 it is immediate, so we assume correctness up to n-1 and prove for ngeq 2. Let g,D as defined in the lemma, and let n>mgeq 1. By choice of g and D, we can select an optimal and truthful bracketsm,D,g,c_m^D,g-auction aucA_m with x[aucA_m]vinset1,m for all vinV. Denote the threshold of alloc[aucA_m] with t_m, and the matching total payments with p_1,p_m such that: x[aucA_m]v= 1,&v<t_m\\ m,&t_mleq v \ \ \ \ textnormaland\ \ \ \ \ \ p[aucA_m]v= p_1,&v<t_m\\ p_m,&t_mleq v . Additionally, denote the corresponding filters with f_m. We first make an observation that will aid as in the design of a new auction. Let v<t_m. We know that either v<f_m or mv-p_mleq v-p_1. If mv-p_mleq v-p_1 it follows that vleq(p_m-p_1)/(m-1)leq p_m. So either way, p_mgeq t_m. We design an n-auction as follows: x[aucA_n]v= 1,& v<t_m\\ n,& vgeq t_m . For bids v such that x[aucA_m]v= 1 we keep p[aucA_n]v=p[aucA_m]v=p_1. For larger bids, the payment rule is a bit more complicated: item The total payment will be p[aucA_n]v=p_ncoloneqfracnmp_m item The payment for the first day will be the filter: f[aucA_n]v=f_ncoloneq t_m That is, the filter is the lowest valuation of agent who is allocated m units in aucA_m. Indeed it's possible, as we observed that t_mleq p_mleq fracnmp_m. item The payment for the subsequent units will be fixed-ratexspace and amount to the remaining payment due. That is, for units 2,dots,n the payment will be fracp_n-f_nn-1 each day. We will show truthfulness of aucA_n. Consider some vinV. item If v<t_m, the agent can only bid below t_m=f_n, which will always result in the same outcome: 1 unit for payment p_1. Hence in this case, agent v is truthful. item If vgeq t_m, we have: util[aucA_n]vv=x[aucA_n]vv-p[aucA_n]v=nv-fracnmp_m=fracnmutil[aucA_m]vvgeq util[aucA_m]vv. Since in aucA_m agent v is truthful, and besides for bidding v there is no other bid in aucA_n that would give a different outcome compared to aucA_m, this proves that also in aucA_n agent v is truthful. nodes.statement: Clearly a rental mechanism in our setting over n days can get an expected reward of at least 0.5n by renting the asset to every agent for a single day, each day getting a reward of bbE[v]=0.5. We now prove the first point using Algorithm~, which we showed is optimal among all fixed-ratexspace SWACsxspace in Theorem~. Denoting D=Uni[0,1], the virtual value for revenue is varphi(v)=v-frac1-v1=2v-1. The virtual value for consumer surplus is varphi_g^D(v)=v-brackets2v-1=1-v. This is a decreasing function of v. Applying the ironing process steps by step gives Barvarphi_g^D(v)=0.5. The lower bound for allocation 1 is bracketsBarvarphi_g^D^-1(0)=0, as we defined the inverse function. We now want to calculate the upper bound, which we denote U. By the first definition of last\_right in Algorithm~, for n=1 clearly all valuations will get an allocation of 1, so we can move on to n>1. Observe that an (n_1+n_2)-rental mechanism with i.i.d. distributions can consist of two shorter rental mechanisms with horizons n_1 and n_2, such that the agents in the first rental mechanism are not allocated the asset past the first n_1 days, in which the first rental mechanism is applied, and after n_1 days the second rental mechanism is applied. Therefore, using the induction hypothesis, for any xinset1,dots,n, fracR_n-1-R_n-xx-1geqfracR_x-1x-1geqfrac12. This means that bracketsBarvarphi_g^D^-1(U)geqbracketsBarvarphi_g^D^-1(0.5)=1. Therefore, all agents are allocated 1 unit in the SWACxspace with n units, which gives a reward of bbE[v]-0=0.5. Due to the algorithm's optimality among fixed-ratexspace SWACsxspace, we are done proving the optimal among fixed-ratexspace SWACxspace. In terms of a rental mechanism that is fixed-ratexspace-optimal, observe that since at every horizon it is optimal for the designer to rent to the agent for a single day for free (as we just proved), the rental mechanism would yield an expected reward of ncdotbbE[v]=0.5n.

Clearly a rental mechanism in our setting over $n$ days can get an expected reward of at least $0.5n$ by renting the asset to every agent for a single day, each day getting a reward of $\bb{E}[v]=0.5$.

    We now prove the first point using Algorithm~\ref{alg:fr-rental}, which we showed is optimal among all fixed-rate\xspace SWACs\xspace in Theorem~\ref{thm:optima-fr-rental-mech}. Denoting $\mathcal{D}=\mathsf{Uni}[0,1]$, the virtual value for revenue is $\varphi(v)=v-\frac{1-v}{1}=2v-1$. The virtual value for consumer surplus is $\varphi_{g}^{\mathcal{D}}(v)=v-\brackets{2v-1}=1-v$. This is a \emph{decreasing} function of $v$. Applying the ironing process steps by step gives $\Bar{\varphi}_{g}^{\mathcal{D}}(v)=0.5$. 

    The lower bound for allocation $1$ is $\brackets{\Bar{\varphi}_{g}^{\mathcal{D}}}^{-1}(0)=0$, as we defined the inverse function. We now want to calculate the upper bound, which we denote $U$. By the first definition of $last\_right$ in Algorithm~\ref{alg:cal-intervals}, for $n=1$ clearly all valuations will get an allocation of $1$, so we can move on to $n>1$. Observe that an $(n_1+n_2)$-rental mechanism with i.i.d. distributions can consist of two shorter rental mechanisms with horizons $n_1$ and $n_2$, such that the agents in the first rental mechanism are not allocated the asset past the first $n_1$ days, in which the first rental mechanism is applied, and after $n_1$ days the second rental mechanism is applied. Therefore, using the induction hypothesis, for any $x\in\set{1,\dots,n}$,
    \begin{align*}
        \frac{R_{n-1}-R_{n-x}}{x-1}\geq\frac{R_{x-1}}{x-1}\geq\frac{1}{2}.
    \end{align*}
    This means that $\brackets{\Bar{\varphi}_{g}^{\mathcal{D}}}^{-1}(U)\geq\brackets{\Bar{\varphi}_{g}^{\mathcal{D}}}^{-1}(0.5)=1$. Therefore, all agents are allocated 1 unit in the SWAC\xspace with $n$ units, which gives a reward of $\bb{E}[v]-0=0.5$. Due to the algorithm's optimality among fixed-rate\xspace SWACs\xspace, we are done proving the optimal among fixed-rate\xspace SWAC\xspace.

    In terms of a rental mechanism that is fixed-rate\xspace-optimal, observe that since at every horizon it is optimal for the designer to rent to the agent for a single day for free (as we just proved), the rental mechanism would yield an expected reward of $n\cdot\bb{E}[v]=0.5n$.

nodes.statement: Let aucA be a deterministic SWACxspace (w.l.o.g. due to Lemma~). Let vinV. If agent v has a pure strategy, denote x_v=xhat[aucA]v (this is a constant) and denote by p_v_1,dots,p_v_x_v the payment schedule of v in aucA. Otherwise, agent v has a mixed strategy that is a convex combination of different strategies. Since aucA is deterministic, there is a single strategy s_v with allocation x_v and payment schedule p_v_1,dots,p_v_x_v that results in at least as much utility for v as the mixed strategy. Define a new SWACxspace aucA' that accepts a single bid from V at the beginning of the auction. For a bid vinV it allocates x_v units, and the payment schedule is exactly p_v_1,dots,p_v_x_v. It is easy to see that aucA' takes the simplified SWACxspace form and that it is truthful, since all agents can get at least as much utility in aucA' by bidding truthfully as they did in aucA, and there are no new payment schedules (so there is no new option that was not available in aucA'). For an agent v with pure strategy we have trew[aucA']v=trew[aucA]v exactly, as the outcomes are exactly the same. For an agent v with mixed strategy, a distribution over a set of strategies Sigma, suppose for the sake of contradiction that trew[aucA']v<trew[aucA]v. Since trew[aucA']v=rew[aucA]vs_v, there is a subset Sigma^astsubseteqSigma of strategies with PrsqbrSigma^ast that result in higher designer reward than s_v. Let s^astinSigma^ast. Since tie-breaking is in favor of the designer, we get that util[aucA]vs^ast<util[aucA]vs_v. But this contradicts the utility-maximization of v in aucA, because removing Sigma^ast from the pool of strategies v might play in aucA would strictly increase v's utility in aucA. Therefore we deduce that trew[aucA']vgeqtrew[aucA]v, resulting in bbEsqbraucA'geqbbEsqbraucA.

nodes.statement: Let mopt be an optimal mechanism in the (n,boldsymbolD,g)-rental game. Recall that mopt is a mapping from a history, which also reflects the current horizon, to a stagewise auction with the corresponding number of units (i.e. at horizon h we get an h-unit auction). We will prove by induction on h (from 0 to n) that the rental mechanism bracketsmopt,dots,mopt,aucA_h,dots,aucA_1 is optimal. The base of horizon 0 is immediate. Now suppose the claim is true for horizons below h and prove for h. By the induction hypothesis, the rental mechanism mechM^1=bracketsmopt,dots,mopt,aucA_h-1,dots,aucA_1 is optimal. We now analyze the mechanism mechM^2=bracketsmopt,dots,mopt,aucA_h,dots,aucA_1=bracketsmechM^1_-h,aucA_h and prove that it is also optimal. For an illustration of mechM^1 and mechM^2 see figure~. [H] [t]0.47textwidth includegraphics[width=textwidth]figures/fig1.PNG captionRental mechanism mechM^1, which is optimal [t]0.5textwidth includegraphics[width=textwidth]figures/fig2.PNG captionRental mechanism mechM^2 caption[A comparison of mechanisms designed in the proof of history-independent rental mechanisms being w.l.o.g.]A comparison of mechM^1 and mechM^2 For any auction aucA, denote by G^aucA(v) the gross reward of the auction, given an agent v and history H_h. Specifically: G^aucA(v)=xhat[aucA]vgbracketsv,fracphat[aucA]vxhat[aucA]v=trew[aucA]v+cbracketsxhat[aucA]v Fix the valuations of the agents arriving in the rental game, and denote them according to their horizon: v_n,dots,v_1. We prove by backwards induction on the horizon that, for all lin seth+1,dots,n+1: item H^mechM^1_l-1=H^mechM^2_l-1, item G^mechM^1(H_l)(v_l)=G^mechM^2(H_l)(v_l) for lleq n (superscripts in the histories omitted due Item~), and item ind[mechM^1]l-1=ind[mechM^2]l-1. This will essentially show that mechM^1 and mechM^2 will behave exactly the same until horizon h and yield the same reward from the first n-h+1 agents. This is very intuitive since for all lin seth+1,dots,n+1, we have mechM^1(H_l)=mopt(H_l)=mechM^2(H_l), but we will prove it formally. The induction is backwards on the horizon, which means that it goes forwards with the timesteps, from before the rental begins, and until horizon h+1. If h=n this is immediate, since in this case mechM^1 and mechM^2 are identical, so suppose h<n. For the base of l=n+1 this is trivial. Suppose the claim is true for horizons l>t, and prove for tin seth+1,dots,n. By the induction hypothesis, ind[mechM^1]t=ind[mechM^2]t, so omit the superscript for simplicity. If indt=0, all items in the claim follow immediately. If indt=1, since both mechanisms are deterministic (as they're truthful), and l>h, we have that the auctions mechM^1(H_t) and mechM^2(H_t) are identical, thus the agents bids will be identical in either case, and so will the auction outcomes, proving the claim for l=t. In particular, we deduce from this that: &sumoflh+1nG^mechM^1(H_l)(v_l)=sumoflh+1nG^mechM^2(H_l)(v_l),\\ &indhcoloneqind[mechM^1]h=ind[mechM^2]h,textnormal and\\ &H_hcoloneqH^mechM^1_h=H^mechM^2_h Analyzing the total reward of mechanism mechM^2, we split to cases depending on indh. If indh=0, then since the histories prior to horizon h were the same in either mechanism, and the realized auctions were the same, then the next timestep in which the asset becomes available will be identical in either case. Since the auctions in mechM^1 and mechM^2 after horizon h are identical, and due to Equation~, we have that trew[mechM^2]v_n,dots,v_1=trew[mechM^1]v_n,dots,v_1. If indh=1 we have, due to the above claim: trew[mechM^2]v_n,dots,v_1&=sumoflh+1nG^mechM^2(H_l)(v_l)+G^mechM^2(H_h)(v_h)+sumofl1h-1G^mechM^2bracketsH_l^mechM^2(v_l)\\ &=sumoflh+1nG^mechM^1(H_l)(v_l)+G^aucA_h(v_h)+sumofl1h-1aucA_l(v_l)\\ &geqsumoflh+1nG^mechM^1(H_l)(v_l)+G^mechM^1(H_h)(v_h)+sumofl1h-1aucA_l(v_l)\\ &=sumoflh+1nG^mechM^1(H_l)(v_l)+G^mechM^1(H_h)(v_h)+sumofl1h-1G^mechM^1bracketsH_l^mechM^1(v_l)\\ &=trew[mechM^1_-h]v_n,dots,v_1 The inequality holds due to our induction hypothesis, that aucA_h-1,dots,aucA_1 are subgame optimal (h-1)-rental mechanism, and since aucA_h is subgame optimal. Since trew[mechM^2]v_n,dots,v_1geqtrew[mechM^1]v_n,dots,v_1 for any realization of agents' valuations, we have bbE[mechM^2]geqbbE[mechM^1]=bbE[mopt], which proves that mechM^2 is indeed optimal and completes the proof.

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{lemma:rental_history_independent}
Any rental mechanism
$\mech{M}$
can be converted
into a rental mechanism $\mech{M}'$,
such that
\begin{enumerate}
\item The designer's expected reward does not change, i.e. $\bb{E}\sqbr{\mech{M}}=\bb{E}\sqbr{\mech{M}'}$ ,
and
\item $\mech{M'}$ is history-independent.
\end{enumerate}

nodes.statement: For simplicity, in this proof we write c_h instead of c_h^boldsymbolD_last h,g and R_h instead of R_h^boldsymbolD_last h,g. Recall that R_h^boldsymbolD_last h,g represents the expected reward from the final h days, using an optimal (h,D_last h,g) rental mechanism. Suppose the claim is false. Thus there is a horizon h and an optimal bracketsh,D_h,g,c-auction which we call aucA, such that aucA is not subgame optimal. Thus, by definition of subgame optimal, there are subgame optimal auctions aucA_h,dots,aucA_1 such that bbEsqbrbracketsaucA,aucA_h-1,dots,aucA_1<bbEsqbrbracketsaucA_h,aucA_h-1,dots,aucA_1 The last transition is due to Lemma~. It holds that, since A_h-1,dots,aucA_1 are subgame optimal: bbEsqbraucA_h,aucA_h-1,dots,aucA_1&=bbEsqbraucA_h(v_h)+sumoflh-11ind[aucA_h,aucA_h-1,dots,aucA_1]laucA_l(v_l)\\ &=bbEsqbraucA_h(v_h)+sumofl1h-maxsetxhat[aucA_h]v_h,1ind[aucA_h,aucA_h,dots,aucA_1]laucA_l(v_l)medspace | medspaceind[aucA_h,aucA_h,dots,aucA_1]h-maxsetxhat[aucA_h]v_h,1=1\\ &=bbEsqbraucA_h(v_h)+trew[aucA_h-maxsetxhat[aucA_h]v_h,1,dots,aucA_1]v_h-maxsetxhat[aucA_h]v_h,1,dots,v_1\\ &=bbEsqbraucA_h(v_h)+R_h-maxsetxhat[aucA_h]v_h,1 And in the same manner, then using the over-time cost function of aucA: bbEsqbraucA,aucA_h-1,dots,aucA_1&=bbEsqbraucA_h(v_h)+R_h-maxsetxhat[aucA]v_h,1\\ &=bbEsqbrtrew[aucA]v_h+R_n-1 Define an auction aucA_h' which follows aucA_h exactly, but its reward is with respect to the cost function is c_h (i.e.\ same auction, different setting). Due to the optimality of aucA, extending Eq.~ we have: bbEsqbraucA,aucA_h-1,dots,aucA_1 &geqbbEsqbrtrew[aucA_h']v_h+R_n-1\\ &=bbEsqbraucA_h'(v_h)-R_n+1+R_h-maxsetxhat[aucA_h']v_h,1+R_n-1\\ &underbrace=_bbEsqbraucA_h(v_h)+R_h-maxsetxhat[aucA_h]v_h,1\\ &underbrace=_bbEsqbraucA_h',aucA_h-1,dots,aucA_1, but this is a contradiction to Eq.~, completing the proof.

Since it follows aucA_h we also have: &bbEsqbraucA_h',aucA_h-1,dots,aucA_1=bbEsqbraucA_h,aucA_h-1,dots,aucA_1>bbEsqbraucA,aucA_h-1,dots,aucA_1 and bbEsqbraucA_h',aucA_h-1,dots,aucA_1=bbEsqbraucA_h'(v_h)+R_h-maxsetxhat[aucA_h']v_h,1=bbEsqbraucA_h(v_h)+R_h-maxsetxhat[aucA_h]v_h,1. Due to the optimality of aucA, extending Eq.~ we have: bbEsqbraucA,aucA_h-1,dots,aucA_1 &geqbbEsqbrtrew[aucA_h']v_h+R_n-1\\ &=bbEsqbraucA_h'(v_h)-R_n+1+R_h-maxsetxhat[aucA_h']v_h,1+R_n-1\\ &underbrace=_bbEsqbraucA_h(v_h)+R_h-maxsetxhat[aucA_h]v_h,1\\ &underbrace=_bbEsqbraucA_h',aucA_h-1,dots,aucA_1, but this is a contradiction to Eq.~, completing the proof.

nodes.name: Ironed virtual valuations~\cite{myerson1981optimal,HartlineR08}
nodes.statement: Given a distribution function F(cdot) and any function theta:VrightarrowR, the textnormalironed virtual value function, Bartheta, is constructed as follows: item For qin[0,1], define h(q)=thetabracketsF^-1(q). item Define H(q)=int_0^q h(r)dr. item Define Psi as the convex hull of H --- the largest convex function bounded above by H for all qin[0,1]. item Define psi(q) as the derivative of Psi(q), where defined, and extend to all of [0,1] by right-continuity. item Finally, Bartheta(v)=psi(F(v)).
nodes.clean_text: Given a distribution function F(cdot) and any function theta:VrightarrowR, the textnormalironed virtual value function, Bartheta, is constructed as follows: item For qin[0,1], define h(q)=thetabracketsF^-1(q). item Define H(q)=int_0^q h(r)dr. item Define Psi as the convex hull of H --- the largest convex function bounded above by H for all qin[0,1]. item Define psi(q) as the derivative of Psi(q), where defined, and extend to all of [0,1] by right-continuity. item Finally, Bartheta(v)=psi(F(v)).
nodes.label: def:ironing

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma~\ref{lemma:irn-maximizer-maximizes-expected}
nodes.statement: Let S be a SWACxspace setting, and theta:VrightarrowR be a function, and Bartheta its ironing Let alloc be a monotone non-decreasing allocation rule that is pointwise maximizing of Bartheta(v)xv-cbracketsxV. Define Psi,H from the ironing procedure used to define Bartheta(cdot). At points v where Psi(F(v))<H(F(v)), Psi is locally linear as the convex hull of H, and hence Bartheta(v) is locally constant. Thus from Lemma~ we are guaranteed that fracddvxv=0 at all such points. It follows that bbEsqbrtheta(v)xv=bbEsqbrBartheta(v)xv. Therefore, also due to xcdot being pointwise maximizing w.r.t. Bartheta, the following expression bbEsqbrtheta(v)xv-cbracketsxv is maximized among all monotone non-decreasing allocation rules.
